title: Final: binary search
sub: Spot a boundary or a search on the answer, predict a trace, find the overflow, explain out loud
cards/0/q: First Bad Version (#278): versions 1..n, n up to 2³¹ − 1. isBadVersion(v) is an expensive request to the build server; after the first bad version all later ones are bad too. Find the first bad one with the fewest requests. Which technique?
cards/0/options/0: The “least x such that true” template on [1, n]: about 31 requests
cards/0/options/1: Scan from the end while versions are bad
cards/0/options/2: Two pointers moving towards each other from both ends
cards/0/options/3: A hash set of already checked versions
cards/0/explain: isBadVersion is monotonic: false…false, true…true, and we need the first true — a lower_bound over a predicate. log₂(2³¹) = 31 requests. The middle must be lo + (hi − lo) / 2: with n near int.MaxValue the sum lo + hi overflows.
cards/0/wrong/1: If the very first version is bad, scanning from the end makes 2³¹ requests. Monotonicity lets you discard half per request.
cards/0/wrong/2: Converging pointers move one step at a time — O(n) requests. What is needed here is the middle, not the ends.
cards/0/wrong/3: Versions are never re-checked anyway; the request count is set by the strategy, and a scan stays O(n).

cards/1/pairs/0/0: How many events of a sorted log fall into [t1, t2]

cards/2/task: A new array: search for 9 in [20, 26, 30, 33, 48, 53, 58, 59, 1, 6, 17] — it is not there. Step through the trace; the rig will stop once and ask what the code does.
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Right [1..17] is sorted, 9 is in it → lo = mid + 1
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Right [1..17] is sorted, 9 is in it → hi = mid − 1
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Left [58..1] is sorted, 9 is in it → hi = mid − 1
cards/2/goal/asks/0/q: The candidates are indices [6..10]: 58, 59, 1, 6, 17. mid = 8, a[mid] = 1. What does the code do?
cards/2/goal/asks/0/explain: a[lo] = 58 > 1 — the drop is on the left, so the right half [1, 6, 17] is sorted. 1 < 9 ≤ 17 — target can only be in it, without mid: lo = 9. In [6, 17] there will be no nine: lo overtakes hi, and the code returns −1 — after four probes out of eleven elements.
cards/3/q: Koko Eating Bananas: up to 10⁴ piles, each up to 10⁹. On large tests the function sometimes returns a speed that is too small. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/3/explain: For a small k the hours reach 10⁴ · 10⁹ = 10¹³, while int holds 2.1·10⁹: the sum wraps around and can turn negative. Then hours <= h holds for a speed that actually does not make it, and hi moves left past the answer. It needs long hours: the check stays monotonic only if it is computed honestly.
cards/4/q: Experience thresholds per level: [0, 100, 250, 500, 1000]. The player has exactly 500 xp. What is their level (threshold index), and which formula gives it?
cards/4/explain: The level is the last threshold not greater than xp. UpperBound(500) = 4 — the first threshold greater than 500, which is 1000; one to the left is 500, index 3. Exactly on the threshold the level is already reached.
cards/4/wrong/1: LowerBound(500) = 3 — the first threshold ≥ 500, the threshold itself. Minus one gives 2: the formula is wrong exactly at the boundary.
cards/4/wrong/2: UpperBound is the first threshold greater than xp, i.e. the next level, not the current one.
cards/4/wrong/3: 500 is in the array, so Array.BinarySearch returns 3 — a non-negative number. ~3 − 1 = −5: “insertion point minus one” is only for a miss.
cards/5/q: A replay: loot must match by seed, but AI and particles also call UnityEngine.Random. What do you do?
cards/5/options/0: Give loot its own generator seeded from the replay — System.Random or Unity.Mathematics.Random
cards/5/options/2: Use the float version of Random.Range instead of the int one
cards/5/options/3: Roll loot in LateUpdate instead of Update
cards/5/explain: UnityEngine.Random has one sequence for everyone: however many numbers AI and particles take, that is how far loot shifts. An instance with explicit state called only by the loot system makes the same seed and the same input produce the same drop.
cards/5/wrong/1: InitState only sets the start of the sequence. Particles and AI still take numbers from the same stream afterwards.
cards/5/wrong/2: The type of the returned number does not change the fact that the stream is shared.
cards/5/wrong/3: LateUpdate also runs once per frame and uses the same shared generator — it fixes neither the order nor the number of calls.
cards/6/q: Split Array Largest Sum (#410): split an array of non-negative numbers into k contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is minimal. What are the bounds for the search on the answer?
cards/6/explain: A part cannot weigh less than the heaviest element — it lands in some part whole. And at x = sum(nums) one part is enough, so fits(hi) is guaranteed to be true. These are the same bounds as for packages within D days.
cards/6/wrong/1: At x = max(nums) more than k parts may be needed — fits(hi) is not guaranteed, and the template returns a wrong answer.
cards/6/wrong/2: sum / k is a lower estimate of the answer, not an upper one: at x = sum / k a split into k parts can be impossible.
cards/6/wrong/3: The answer is often above max(nums) — a part usually holds more than one element — and then it is outside the range: fits(hi) is not guaranteed.
cards/7/q: A new problem: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (#1011). Put the steps of the out-loud explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: is the package order fixed? Can a package be split? What are n and the weights?
cards/7/items/1: Naive: try capacities from max to sum, checking each in O(n)
cards/7/items/2: Idea: “is cap enough” is monotonic — search for the first true on [max, sum]
cards/7/items/3: Code: a greedy check by days and the template hi = mid, lo = mid + 1
cards/7/items/4: Run weights 1..10 with D = 5: the answer is 15
cards/7/items/5: Complexity: O(n log(sum)) time, O(1) memory
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: D = 1 — the answer is sum, D = n — the answer is max, a single package
cards/7/explain: The same script as for Koko — only the check changes. The edge cases D = 1 and D = n also verify the bounds: the answer can coincide with either of them.
cards/8/q: What is true about complexity? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: lower_bound in an array of 10⁹ elements takes about 30 iterations
cards/8/options/1: Koko Eating Bananas is O(n log max(piles))
cards/8/options/2: Median of two arrays with the cut is O(log min(m, n))
cards/8/options/3: Search in a rotated array with duplicates is O(log n) in the worst case
cards/8/options/5: A loot table on prefix sums: building O(n), a pick O(log n)
cards/8/explain: log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30. Koko is about log₂ max checks of O(n) each. The cut is searched over the shorter array. With duplicates the worst case is O(n): in ones with a single two every cell has to be inspected. Fisher–Yates is a single pass of swaps: O(n). Prefixes are one pass, a pick is one upper_bound.
